canonical_topic: Acid rain from nitrogen and sulfur oxides
definition: Combustion also produces nitrogen and sulfur oxides — from atmospheric nitrogen and trace sulfur trapped in fossil fuels — which combine with water to form acid rain, a regional hazard to vegetation and wildlife when concentrated.
core_idea: Nitrogen and sulfur oxides released by combustion react with water to create acid rain, which is normally mild but becomes locally poisonous when acid accumulates heavily in one area.
key_points: Nitrogen oxides come from atmospheric nitrogen; sulfur oxides come from trace sulfur trapped in fossil fuels.
These oxides combine with water to form acid rain.
Acid rain is characterized as a regional problem that can kill vegetation and wildlife.
Most rain is slightly acidic already; the hazard arises when large amounts of acid concentrate in a small area.
relationships: Two general categories of combustion pollution
caveats: Assuming all acid rain is dangerous — the author notes most rain is mildly acidic and only concentrated buildup is poisonous.
